title: Testing Before Scaling
text:
Governments are often in a hurry. A problem appears in the headlines, ministers promise action, and a programme is launched across the whole country within months. The instinct is understandable, for delay can look like indifference. Yet the history of public policy is crowded with schemes that were well intentioned, expensive and largely ineffective, and many of them failed for reasons that a modest trial would have revealed.

The case for piloting a policy before scaling it up rests on a simple observation: the people who design a programme rarely know in advance how citizens, officials and markets will respond to it. A subsidy meant for poor households may be captured by intermediaries; a school meal scheme may raise attendance in one district and have no effect in another where children stay home for different reasons. A pilot, run in a limited area and compared honestly with similar areas that did not receive the programme, turns such guesses into evidence.

Pilots are not without their critics. Some argue that they are slow, and that withholding a promising benefit from some communities is unfair. Others point out that a scheme which succeeds on a small scale, under the eye of enthusiastic officials, may disappoint when it is handed to an ordinary bureaucracy. These objections are serious, but they argue for designing pilots carefully rather than abandoning them. A trial can be run in stages so that every area eventually receives the benefit, and it can be managed by the same officials who would run the national scheme.

What pilots demand, above all, is humility. To test a policy is to admit that it might not work, and politicians are seldom rewarded for such admissions. But a government that learns from a small failure is spared a large one, and public money, which is always scarce, is spent where it actually makes a difference.

title: The Invisible Economy
text:
In many developing countries, the greater part of working life takes place outside the reach of official statistics. The street vendor, the home-based tailor, the mechanic who repairs motorcycles under a tree and the labourer hired by the day are rarely registered, seldom taxed and almost never protected by labour law. Economists call this the informal economy, and for a long time it was treated as a temporary stage that would disappear as countries grew richer.

That expectation has not been fulfilled. In a number of economies informal work has persisted, and in some it has grown, even during periods of rapid growth. The reasons are not mysterious. Registering a business can involve lengthy procedures, repeated visits to offices and payments that a small trader cannot afford. Taxes and regulations designed for large firms fall heavily on small ones. For many workers, informality is less a choice than the only door that is open.

It would be a mistake, however, to regard the informal economy merely as a problem. It absorbs millions who would otherwise have no income, supplies cheap goods and services to poorer households, and nurtures skills and enterprise in places the formal sector does not reach. At the same time, its costs are real. Informal workers have little security against illness, old age or a bad season, their firms struggle to borrow and grow, and the state loses revenue it needs for schools and hospitals.

The sensible response is neither to romanticise informality nor to attack it. Heavy-handed crackdowns on vendors and workshops usually destroy livelihoods without creating better ones. A more patient approach lowers the cost of becoming formal, simplifies taxes for small enterprises and extends basic social protection to those who remain outside the system. Formality, in other words, should be made attractive rather than compulsory.

title: Print and the Spread of Knowledge
text:
Before the arrival of printing, a book was a rare and costly object. Every copy had to be written out by hand, a task that could occupy a skilled scribe for months, and errors crept in with each new copy. Libraries were small, and learning was concentrated in the hands of those institutions and families that could afford to maintain them. Knowledge travelled, but it travelled slowly and unevenly.

Printing did not begin in Europe. Techniques for printing from carved wooden blocks were in use in East Asia centuries earlier, and movable type had been developed there as well. But when a system of movable metal type spread across Europe in the fifteenth century, it combined with a growing demand for books, the availability of paper and an expanding network of trade. The result was a sharp fall in the cost of reproducing texts and a steady rise in the number of books in circulation.

The consequences reached far beyond the workshop. Identical copies allowed scholars in distant cities to refer to the same page and to correct the same errors, so that knowledge could accumulate rather than decay. Pamphlets carried arguments on religion and politics to readers who had never entered a university. Standardised printed texts gradually helped to fix spelling and grammar in several languages, and cheaper books encouraged more people to learn to read.

Historians caution against treating printing as the single cause of all that followed. Literacy spread slowly, many people continued to rely on the spoken word, and the new technology could spread falsehood and bitter polemic as easily as sound learning. Nevertheless, by making the written word cheaper, more stable and more widely available, printing changed the conditions under which ideas were formed, tested and shared.

title: The Life Beneath Our Feet
text:
We walk on soil every day and rarely give it a thought. To most people it is simply dirt, an inert layer in which plants happen to stand. Soil scientists see something very different: a living system, as complex in its way as a forest or a coral reef, on which almost all of our food ultimately depends.

A handful of healthy soil contains an astonishing variety of organisms. Bacteria and fungi break down dead leaves, roots and animal remains, releasing the nutrients that plants need to grow. Earthworms and other small creatures burrow through the ground, mixing it and opening channels through which air and water can move. Fungal threads wrap around plant roots and extend their reach, exchanging minerals for sugars that the plants produce. Far from being a passive medium, soil is the scene of constant exchange.

This living quality also makes soil fragile. Soil forms extremely slowly, as rock weathers and organic matter builds up over long periods, yet it can be lost quickly. When land is left bare, wind and rain carry away the fertile top layer. Heavy machinery compacts the ground and squeezes out the air that organisms need. Excessive use of chemical inputs can harm the very organisms that keep the soil productive, so that farmers find themselves applying more and more to obtain the same harvest.

None of this means that modern farming must be abandoned. It means that soil should be managed as a resource to be conserved rather than a surface to be exploited. Practices such as keeping the ground covered with crops or residues, rotating crops and returning organic matter to the land help to protect soil structure and the life within it. A society that looks after its soil is, quite literally, securing its own foundations.

subject: English
q: The author’s central argument is that governments should:
o: test policies on a limited scale before introducing them nationwide
avoid launching new programmes until public demand is overwhelming
hand the design of welfare schemes to independent experts
replace subsidies with school meal programmes
explanation: The passage builds the case for piloting a policy before scaling it up, arguing that a small trial turns guesses into evidence and spares a government a large failure.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, a subsidy meant for poor households may fail because it:
o: raises attendance in only one district
is withheld from some communities
is run by enthusiastic officials
may be captured by intermediaries
explanation: The second paragraph states that a subsidy meant for poor households ‘may be captured by intermediaries’, so it does not reach the intended people.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is mentioned in the passage as a criticism of pilot programmes?
o: Pilots cost more public money than national schemes
A scheme that succeeds on a small scale may disappoint when run by an ordinary bureaucracy
Pilots make politicians unpopular with voters
Pilot areas cannot be compared with areas that did not receive the programme
explanation: The third paragraph reports critics’ point that success ‘under the eye of enthusiastic officials’ may not survive being handed to an ordinary bureaucracy; the other options are not raised as criticisms.

subject: English
q: The word ‘captured’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: taken over
imprisoned
recorded
attracted
explanation: A subsidy ‘captured by intermediaries’ is one that middlemen take over for their own benefit instead of letting it reach poor households.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author regards the objections to pilots as:
o: decisive arguments against testing policies
irrelevant to the use of public money
reasons to design pilots more carefully rather than to drop them
concerns raised mainly by politicians
explanation: The author calls the objections ‘serious’ but says they ‘argue for designing pilots carefully rather than abandoning them’, and then shows how staging and staffing can answer them.

subject: English
q: The author’s attitude towards governments that launch nationwide schemes in haste is best described as:
o: openly contemptuous
understanding but critical
wholly approving
indifferent
explanation: The author concedes that the instinct to act quickly ‘is understandable’ yet points to the many expensive failures such haste has produced, which is sympathetic but critical.

subject: English
q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: Why Street Vendors Should Be Removed
The End of Informal Work
Taxing Large Firms Fairly
The Informal Economy: Burden and Lifeline
explanation: The passage weighs the informal economy’s benefits (income, cheap goods, enterprise) against its costs (insecurity, lost revenue), so a title combining ‘burden’ and ‘lifeline’ fits best.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, which of the following discourages small traders from registering their businesses?
o: A lack of demand for their goods
Lengthy procedures and payments they cannot afford
The protection offered by labour law
Competition from foreign firms
explanation: The second paragraph says registration ‘can involve lengthy procedures, repeated visits to offices and payments that a small trader cannot afford’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, one cost of the informal economy to the state is that:
o: it must pay pensions to informal workers
it has to lend money to small firms
it is forced to close down workshops
it loses revenue needed for schools and hospitals
explanation: The third paragraph lists among the costs of informality that ‘the state loses revenue it needs for schools and hospitals’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘romanticise’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: idealise
criticise
legalise
ignore
explanation: To ‘romanticise’ informality is to present it as better than it is; the author pairs it with ‘attack’ as the two extremes to avoid.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author believes informality persists mainly because:
o: informal workers prefer to avoid paying any tax
economic growth has stopped in developing countries
the formal system imposes costs that many small businesses cannot bear
governments deliberately encourage it
explanation: The author explains persistence by costly registration and rules ‘designed for large firms’, adding that informality is ‘less a choice than the only door that is open’, which rules out mere tax avoidance.

subject: English
q: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?
o: Crackdowns on street vendors are an effective way to formalise the economy
Informal work will disappear automatically as a country grows richer
Governments should make registration simpler and cheaper for small enterprises
The informal economy imposes no real costs on workers
explanation: The final paragraph recommends lowering the cost of becoming formal and simplifying taxes for small enterprises, and rejects crackdowns as destroying livelihoods.

subject: English
q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: the ways in which printing changed the spread and preservation of knowledge
the invention of paper in East Asia
the decline of universities in the fifteenth century
the working methods of scribes
explanation: Each paragraph traces how printing altered the cost, stability and reach of written knowledge, ending with its effect on how ideas were ‘formed, tested and shared’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, hand-copied books were prone to errors because:
o: scribes were deliberately careless
paper was of poor quality
books had to be translated into several languages
mistakes crept in each time a new copy was made
explanation: The first paragraph says that every copy was written by hand and ‘errors crept in with each new copy’.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, movable metal type had a large effect in Europe partly because it:
o: was the first form of printing anywhere in the world
coincided with growing demand for books, available paper and expanding trade
was supported by every university
replaced the spoken word within a generation
explanation: The second paragraph says the new system ‘combined with a growing demand for books, the availability of paper and an expanding network of trade’; it also states that printing began earlier in East Asia.

subject: English
q: The word ‘polemic’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: fierce argument
careful scholarship
popular poetry
official decree
explanation: ‘Bitter polemic’ is set against ‘sound learning’: it refers to aggressive, one-sided controversy, which printing could spread as easily as scholarship.

subject: English
q: Identical printed copies helped knowledge to ‘accumulate rather than decay’ because:
o: printed books could not be destroyed
pamphlets replaced university teaching
scholars could correct a shared text instead of each copy drifting further from the original
spelling ceased to matter to readers
explanation: Hand copies gathered new errors each time, whereas identical copies let scholars ‘refer to the same page and correct the same errors’, so corrections built up instead of mistakes multiplying.

subject: English
q: The author’s view of the impact of printing can best be described as:
o: uncritically enthusiastic
balanced, acknowledging both its importance and its limits
largely dismissive
nostalgic for the age of manuscripts
explanation: The author credits printing with changing the conditions of intellectual life but, in the last paragraph, warns against treating it as the single cause and notes it spread falsehood too.

subject: English
q: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?
o: The Dangers of Earthworms
Why Modern Farming Must End
How Rocks Are Formed
Soil: A Living and Fragile Resource
explanation: The passage first shows that soil is a living system and then that this makes it fragile and in need of conservation; it explicitly denies that modern farming must be abandoned.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, fungal threads around plant roots:
o: prevent air and water from entering the soil
exchange minerals for sugars produced by the plants
break down rock into sand
compete with plants for sunlight
explanation: The second paragraph says fungal threads extend the roots’ reach, ‘exchanging minerals for sugars that the plants produce’.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is mentioned in the passage as a way in which soil is damaged?
o: Excessive growth of fungi
Rotating crops too often
Covering the ground with crop residues
Heavy machinery compacting the ground
explanation: The third paragraph states that ‘heavy machinery compacts the ground and squeezes out the air that organisms need’; crop rotation and residues are given as protective practices.

subject: English
q: The word ‘inert’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: lifeless and inactive
rich and fertile
heavy and dense
dry and dusty
explanation: Most people see soil as ‘an inert layer’, which the author contrasts with the scientists’ view of it as ‘a living system’, so ‘inert’ means lifeless and inactive.

subject: English
q: The remark that farmers ‘find themselves applying more and more to obtain the same harvest’ suggests that:
o: chemical inputs are becoming cheaper
harvests are increasing every year
overuse of chemicals can gradually weaken the soil’s natural productivity
farmers are unaware of crop rotation
explanation: The remark follows the point that excessive chemical inputs harm the organisms that keep soil productive, so the soil yields less on its own and needs ever larger doses.

subject: English
q: The author’s main purpose in the passage is to:
o: argue that chemical fertilisers should be banned
describe the life cycle of the earthworm
persuade readers to regard soil as a living resource that needs conservation
compare soil with coral reefs in detail
explanation: The passage moves from correcting the view of soil as mere dirt to urging that it be ‘managed as a resource to be conserved rather than a surface to be exploited’.
